source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 14% of people in Belgium were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
26.4% of health spending in Belgium was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
1.3% of people in Belgium reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
13% of hospital care costs in Belgium were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
38% of outpatient medical care costs in Belgium were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
72% of dental care costs in Belgium were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
26% of pharmaceutical costs in Belgium were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
Complementary insurance to cover cost-sharing is widely used in Belgium (97% of the population).

Over the last decade, the population covered by additional private health insurance has increased in 16 of 29 OECD countries with comparable data, with large increases in Belgium and Denmark (over 15 percentage points).

Outpatient care accounted for 22% of household spending on healthcare on average, but was especially high in Belgium (43%), Italy (48%) and Portugal (52%) where cost-sharing arrangements for outpatient care are common.
In general, doctors were more evenly distributed across regions in Belgium, Japan and Korea.

With public health emergency measures phased out after the acute phase of the pandemic, the share of preventive spending dropped and reached pre-pandemic levels by 2023, ranging from 6-7% of total health spending in Canada and the United Kingdom to less than 3% in Poland, Belgium, Iceland, France, Switzerland, Portugal and Japan.

Overall, every third health dollar was spent on ambulatory providers in Belgium, Mexico, Finland, Luxembourg and the United States but this share was below 20% in Türkiye, Greece and the Slovak Republic.
As a result, day care services account for 15% or more of all hospital expenditures in Belgium, Ireland and Portugal.
